With holidays rolling around the corner I thought it would be cool to discuss one of the most important accessories for cigar smokers - the cutter. Before I go into the types of cutters I feel the need to briefly cover how to cut a cigar. One part of the cigar anatomy is the cap. At the very, very least do not cut higher than the cap goes. If you do you run the risk of having the wrapper unravel, which is never fun. You really just want to nip the tip. Cut only as much as you need to get a smooth draw (usually about ~1/8 of an inch).

Cutters come in all shapes and sizes, so I’ll just discuss a few of the most prominent varieties.

  • Guillotine - this is the most common form of cigar cutter. There are a few different types of guillotine cutters (single blade/double blade), but they all function similarly. These are easy to operator and are good for almost every type of cigar. Some things to note: some cigars may have too large of a ring gauge to use a guillotine on. For these I’d recommend a punch or scissors. Also, some guillotine cutters have a solid back on one side. This is designed to ensure you don’t cut off too much.

  • Punch - these are perfect for larger ringed cigars and/or if you don’t plan of putting the whole cap of the cigar in your mouth when you smoke. These are simple to use, but do have some risk as they may end up cracking the foot if not sharp or if used on thinner cigars. They’re also not very useful on torpedoes, belicosos, or chisels (although you can punch the side if you must).

  • V-cut - this cuts a v-shaped chunk out of your cigar cap. This is a good cutter to use if you want a looser draw than using a punch, but still don’t want loose tobacco to get in your mouth.

  • Scissors - this is my cutter of choice as it offers the most flexibility, especially if you use a multitool like the Xikar scissors. I honestly don’t think I’ve used a different type of cutter since I got my scissors. There’s also the most risk associated with these since you have free reign on where/how to cut, but that freedom is what I like most about it.

  • Shuriken - I have no personal experience with this type of cutter, but I thought it should still be listed.

Cutters are one of those things that boils down to personal preference. They make great gifts. And, if you’re really into the hobby, they’re somewhat collectibles (I have accumulated at least 10 different cutters over the years).

Hope this helps. Feel free to discuss and/or chime in if I missed something.

Just the other day I wrote a big long thing about why I feel it's inappropriate (from a political theory standpoint) to use "liberal" and "conservative" as opposites.

Liberalism is about trying to find a form of government that maximizes what I call "real liberty" and changing our society and government to make that happen. This first started a few hundred years ago, when most of Western society was still controlled by monarchs and nobility. When these first liberals started running around and talking about things like individual freedom and property rights and free markets (because this really was new and revolutionary stuff back then), a bunch of people didn't like how quickly the liberals were trying to change things because rapid social change causes turmoil. This second group wrote a bunch of stuff about how there's a reason things are the way they are and how big social change like the liberals want needs to happen slowly if it has to happen at all, so society has time to adjust to the changes as they come. This is where conservatism comes from.

Jump forward in time a few hundred years, and now we're in a society that has had time to adjust to the classical liberal ideas - the US was founded on a lot of these principles, remember - and while today's liberals continue to push for social change in the name of freedom (The birth control pill and abortions allow women to be free from the biological mandate to have a dozen babies, the gay rights movement allowed men to have sex with other men without risking being arrested for it, etc...) modern conservatives are saying things like, "Alright, so personal liberties and free markets really did work out, but we had hundreds of years to adapt to it and now you're asking us to let men use the women's restroom just because they want to be women? That's crazy!"

And that's how I'm in the position of being both a liberal and a conservative. I'm gay, my best friend's transgender, and I'm all for changing society so everything's fair and there may finally be peace and love and harmony, but these changes take time. The truth is, I'm kind of sorry for my trans friend because I look at how wound up society is over all the social change that's happened recently and I'm forced to say, "Some day, we'll be there. Some day, nobody will judge you for who you are and how you want to live. But I've seen the backlash from a society that isn't ready for change yet, and if you try to force change to happen now, it will only end in tears."

It pains me to say it, but it's the truth as far as I can tell. I wasn't even ready for gay marriage, frankly: I had made peace with living with a "boyfriend" or "partner" for the rest of my life, and calling him my "fiance" still freaks me out, even as thankful as I am for it.

So, maybe you're like me. If you fight for equality, if you hope for change, that makes you a liberal. But if you're tired of seeing that fight hurt communities, if you're happy to see that people are moving in the right direction, even if they're moving slowly, you're also a conservative. Don't let people goad you into thinking that you have to pigeonhole yourself into one or the other.
